summary: Oral delayed-release budesonide is a locally acting glucocorticoid used to treat mild-to-moderate active Crohn's disease involving the ileum and/or ascending colon and to maintain remission for up to 3 months. Its high first-pass hepatic metabolism delivers topical anti-inflammatory effect in the gut with fewer systemic corticosteroid effects than prednisolone, though hypercorticism and adrenal suppression can still occur.
indications: Treatment of mild-to-moderate active Crohn's disease involving the ileum and/or ascending colon (patients >=8 years)
Maintenance of clinical remission of mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease involving the ileum and/or ascending colon for up to 3 months (adults)

moa: Budesonide is a high-potency glucocorticoid that binds the glucocorticoid receptor and broadly suppresses inflammatory mediators (cytokines, prostaglandins, leukotrienes) and inflammatory cell activity in the intestinal mucosa. The delayed/controlled-release formulation releases drug in the distal ileum and ascending colon, and extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4) limits systemic glucocorticoid exposure, providing targeted anti-inflammatory action with a relatively favorable systemic profile.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to budesonide or any ingredient (anaphylaxis reported)

monitor: Signs of hypercorticism and adrenal axis suppression

preg: Corticosteroids may have some risk; use oral budesonide in pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Monitor neonates of mothers on corticosteroids for hypoadrenalism.
lact: Budesonide is present in breast milk in small amounts; inhaled/oral local budesonide is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Consider the mother's clinical need and the infant.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is provided for renal impairment.
hepatic: Reduced hepatic clearance increases systemic exposure; consider reducing the dose to 3 mg once daily in moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B) and monitor for systemic corticosteroid effects. Avoid/limit in severe impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, cobicistat) - markedly increase budesonide exposure and systemic corticosteroid effects; avoid
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) - reduce efficacy
Other corticosteroids (additive immunosuppression and adrenal effects)

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is nearly time for the next day's dose, skip it and resume your regular morning schedule. Do not double up.
overdose: Acute overdose is unlikely to cause clinical problems; chronic excessive dosing produces systemic hypercorticism. Manage by reducing the dose gradually (do not stop abruptly) and supportive care.
